blocks.text: *The battle of the Fourteen Kashira against Chaos, told in full — and what it cost them.*
Before the battle

For three moonless nights before anyone else moved, Vael lay on the farthest hill above the field with his rifle across his knees, watching the dark. He had told the others he would fire once, and only when there was something worth hitting. Nobody argued. Vael had never missed, mostly because he had never hurried.
The opening

Chaos came the way bad thoughts come — all at once and from every side. Celestia went first, because somebody had to make it choose a direction. She drifted above it like a passing cloud, never where it reached for her, and rained arrows into it until it lost patience and turned to chase her across the plain.
The river

She led it straight to Orion. He had chosen the ground days earlier: a bend where the land narrowed, the one place the others could meet it together. When it came pouring after Celestia he hooked it with his spear and dragged it, step by step, the way a river bends whatever falls into it, until it stood exactly where he wanted it.
The tide and the earth

Mordane was waiting there. He rose like a raging tide, and one sweep of his greatsword crashed over its front and cleared the road. What survived came back at Orion with everything it had — until Tharos leapt from the ridge and brought his hammer down hard enough, the others swore, to break a falling star. The earth split open under it, and for one breath the whole field stood frozen.
The light

Chaos found its feet and threw itself at the others. Asterion stepped in front of all of them. He took every blow that was meant for someone else — blocked them, turned them back, refused to fall — and when it finally staggered, he gathered every scrap of strength he had left into a single fist. When it landed, the sky above the field lit green and violet, like the northern lights.
The charge

Through that light came Varkhaz. He did not defend and he did not step back. Each blow of his axe caught the next, the way wildfire runs through dry grass, until the dark ahead of him was nothing but a narrowing corridor — and at the end of it, the heart.
The thousand cuts

Veyra was already moving. She dashed past Varkhaz down that corridor, petals streaming behind her, and cut the heart of Chaos a thousand times in a few heartbeats. Veyra had never lost an exchange, and she did not lose this one. The heart died. But as it died, Chaos did what it had planned from the start: it left the heart and fled into the one who had killed it. Veyra fell before the petals settled.
The dew

Seraphine reached her through the storm and knelt beside her. Bringing the fallen back was what Seraphine was for — she had done it a hundred times that night. As the morning mist gathered around them, Veyra opened her eyes and stood. And Seraphine, still holding her hand, felt something cold look back at her out of Veyra's face. She told herself she was tired. She said nothing.
The empty dark

Behind them, the dark kept fighting. Nothing was inside it now, but Chaos left it moving, because a battle that suddenly stopped would have given everything away. It split into a hundred shapes to hold the Fourteen's attention, and Riven answered with a hundred blades, flung and whirling through every one of them like leaves in an autumn gale.
The poison and the ash

In the confusion nobody saw Velmora arrive. She nicked the dark once with a blade wet with nightshade and stepped back to let the poison bloom. It seemed to weaken. Kaelen set the ground beneath it burning, then froze the flames to ash under ice, so it had nowhere left to stand.
The lily

Morwen did nothing quickly. She laid one quiet curse on the dark, as she always did, and waited for it to take hold. It never did. A curse cannot take hold of something with nothing inside it — and Morwen understood what that meant. She looked across the field at Veyra, standing again, and noticed what no one else had: wherever Veyra moved, petals had always fallen. Now they had stopped. Telling no one yet, Morwen laid a second curse, a slow one, on Veyra herself.
The crack

Nysara had been circling the whole time, unseen, a mirage in the dust. When the poison and the ash had done their work, one crack finally showed in the dark. She struck that exact spot, again and again and again, until it split wide.
The shot

On the farthest hill, three nights of waiting ended. Through Nysara's crack Vael fired his one shot out of the dark, and it fell like a star. The seal closed. The battle was over. Fourteen walked home.
After

Morwen did not stay quiet. She stood in front of the others and said that Chaos had not been sealed — that it was here, among them, in Veyra. But her curse had not bloomed yet, and she had nothing to show them. Veyra did not deny it angrily. She turned it around, gently: the curse-caster who sees rot everywhere, accusing the one who had just died for them. Was it not more likely that Chaos had found its way into Morwen? Seraphine knew the truth, but saying it would mean admitting she had brought Chaos home with her own hands, so she stood beside Veyra. One by one, most of the others followed her.
The fear

The artist heard all of it. He could not tell which of his champions was lying, because Chaos is made of his own thoughts, and a thought wearing the face of his own creation feels exactly like his own. Two of his champions accused each other and twelve took sides, any of whom could be fooled, or lying. His doubt did not stop at the two. It reached every one of them, until, in his mind, his fear turned all fourteen into shadows. Chaos never needed to fight him again. Turning him against his own champions had been the attack all along.
The mark

Days later, Morwen's slow curse finally bloomed: a black lily mark on Veyra. But by then there was no Veyra left to show it to — only her shadow. Nobody had ever seen the mark on the Kashira, and the mark is still there on her shadow now. It is the proof. Morwen did the right thing and caused the tragedy anyway, and her shadow is the most bitter of the fourteen.
Now

Thirteen of the shadows are innocent: they are the artist's fear wearing his champions' shapes, and they come back whenever the fear does. The fourteenth is Chaos wearing Veyra's face. The artist cannot sort them out himself. The proof has to come from outside his mind — from the unwritten, remembering each Kashira as they really were, one at a time, on evidence instead of fear.
*Each Kashira's legend in a single line, and their names and styles, are on* **The World of Unwritten**.
